This song from 1982 came on the radio the other day and a line caught my ear: "I've spent my life exploring the subtle whoring..."

Uh oh! She is imploring other women not to repeat her mistake ("I wish someone had talked to me like I wanna talk to you"), and urging tradwives to appreciate what they have rather than buying into the lie of what they're missing out on.

The line actually continues:

I've spent my life exploring the subtle whoring that costs too much to be free

As that wording was considered a little vulgar at the time, there was another version in which the point is even clearer:

I thought my heart would wait but I learned too late that it costs too much to be free

You will be astonished to learn that the song reached #3 in the US, and #1 in Australia, Canada, and the UK. You'll probably share my view that a song with such a message would never be allowed to be successful today, and would probably struggle just to secure any airtime. It was only 35 years ago! I wonder even if the station I heard it on this week would have played it if they knew its content and meaning.

To get a value of 1, for say something like a .308 round this would have to be 0.308 inches above a surface. This would mean that the barrel is resting on the surface, which is not something I would do. At a more reasonable height say 3 inches above a surface like the thickness of the hand that holding the gun, this value would be 10. The paper below, which I have access to is studying the effects with h/d at something like 0.42 which is something like 0.13 inches. This is more applicable to ricochets, which is why they follow walls. Think of it this way, the traveling shock wave would have to reflect off of a surface and still be under the bullet to reflect off the bullet to matter. For a given mach number, i would think a good 1st approximation could be done with trigonometry. This is why h/d must be small, or even less than one to matter. Less than one means closer than the diameter of the bullet. Most normal shooting wont be affected by this.

Doig, G., Barber, T. J., Leonardi, E., Neely, A. J., & Kleine, H. (2010). Aerodynamics of a supersonic projectile in proximity to a solid surface. AIAA journal, 48(12), 2916-2930.

Typically for ground effect to be considered significant you have to be within 1/2 of the wingspan from the surface, which on a .308 bullet is 0.154 inches. A bullet going just barely supersonic will get some destabilizing effects from the shock wave being reflected off the ground if it's down low.
